# What does query fan-out mean?

**Query fan-out is the expansion of a user’s question into related searches across subtopics or sources before a system assembles its response.**


Observed answers on stated dates, not a ranking.
The question a person writes need not be the only search a system issues. An assistant comparing products could investigate compatibility, support and documented limitations separately before assembling an answer. That example illustrates the mechanism; it is not an observed hidden search trace.

For a broader product explanation, read [what Google AI Mode is](/answers/google-ai/what-is-google-ai-mode/). This entry distinguishes fan-out as a retrieval behavior from the measurable answer that follows it.

## A dated operator description

Google’s **5 March 2025** introduction of AI Mode explicitly described query fan-out: concurrent related searches across subtopics and data sources, followed by a combined response. This is the earliest dated operator description using the phrase that we verified for this page, not a claim to have found the origin of every earlier technical use. [Stein, 2025].

Google’s current Search Central guidance says AI Overviews and AI Mode **may** use the technique. It also says the experiences can use different models and techniques. “May” matters: the documentation does not establish that every answer runs the same expansion, or that all engines implement a shared recipe. [Google Search Central, AI features].

The operator describes behavior. It does not provide a publisher with a guaranteed list of future subqueries for an arbitrary question.

## How vendors use the phrase

Zach Paruch’s Semrush article, dated **26 September 2025**, describes updating selected articles to address researched fan-out questions, then comparing tracked answer metrics before and after. The article itself notes that Google’s dynamically generated subqueries cannot be known in advance with certainty. [Paruch, 2025].

That distinction separates an observed search trace from a suggested related-question list. A planning aid may generate useful questions without reproducing what an engine actually searched. Label the list according to how it was obtained.

The Semrush account is a small vendor case, not a general causal estimate. Its baseline describes citation coverage in terms of articles cited at least once, while the result describes citation counts. We do not use the headline increase as a directly comparable treatment-effect statistic without resolving that unit difference.

## What can be measured?

If a collection exposes the searches actually issued, preserve each visible search string with its parent interaction, time and source. State whether the record is complete or only the part the interface exposed. Count interaction-level expansion separately from the number of issued searches.

A final citation list does not reveal all retrieved documents. A system may consider a source without citing it, and a visible link may not tell you which search retrieved it. Reconstructing every hidden query from those links would add evidence the record does not contain.

When actual search traces are unavailable, describe observable outputs: which answers named a brand, which URLs were cited and how those events vary across repeated questions. Do not rename those output counts “fan-out coverage.” They measure a different stage.

## What does the concept change for a publisher?

It gives a sensible reason to answer the supporting questions a reader would need to resolve. A comparison page can explain exclusions and compatibility as well as the headline feature. Keep those sections useful on their own, with the evidence next to the claim.

It does not justify publishing every conceivable wording as a separate page. Thin variants create upkeep. Group related material where it serves the reader, and give genuinely different questions distinct, substantive answers.

Google’s current guidance keeps ordinary Search eligibility relevant to its AI features and promises no guaranteed inclusion. The mechanism supplies context for content planning, not an exemption from evidence, a special ranking formula or a requirement to expose undocumented files.

Google states, “Both AI Overviews and AI Mode may use a ‘query fan-out’ technique”. Its qualified verb leaves room for different responses and implementations; an observed output alone does not expose the complete search process. [Google Search Central, AI features and your website, “How AI features work in Search”; verified 30 October 2026].

## What our own data shows

Source archive: [release 2026-09, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22907695](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22907695).

**Supports:** Our released answer archive supports citation and naming analysis, **not a complete fan-out trace**. Study 2 counted **18,893 citation occurrences in eligible target answers**, separately from **1,297 control-answer occurrences**. These counts describe the saved citation lists, not how many searches generated them.

The [registered citation study](/research/studies/who-ai-engines-cite/) publishes its inclusion rules and source-class tables. Those are the published outcome labels. No result there establishes which unobserved subquery caused a source to be chosen.

**Does not support:** Future rankings or a causal publishing effect.

**Suggests:** Follow-up within the stated setting.

# What does Share of Model measure?

**Share of Model is a brand’s share of category-brand mentions in a specified set of AI answers; the question set and counting rules define the result.**


Observed answers on stated dates, not a ranking.
The capitalized name can refer to a product as well as a marketing measure. Ask for the calculation before comparing two dashboards. A count of answers naming a company and a share of all brand mentions answer different questions, even when both carry the same label.

For practical reporting decisions, use the library’s [client AI visibility report guidance](/answers/measurement/what-should-a-client-ai-visibility-report-contain/). This definition concerns the denominator behind the term.

## Which early uses can we verify?

# What is zero-click visibility?

**Zero-click visibility is a brand or source appearing in a search or generated answer without an observed visit to its website during that interaction.**


Observed answers on stated dates, not a ranking.
A name can be visible even when no website visit follows. That is an exposure event. Establishing that a particular person saw it, understood it or later bought something requires different evidence. The phrase should not collapse all those outcomes into a single measure.

For the practical attribution question, use [the evidence needed to connect AI visibility with pipeline](/answers/measurement/what-evidence-can-connect-ai-visibility-with-pipeline/). This entry concerns what “zero-click” can and cannot mean.

## The older idea and the newer phrase

Rand Fishkin’s SparkToro post dated **13 August 2019** documents the older zero-click-search concept in a browser-panel analysis. Its definition includes searches ending without a website referral for several reasons: an answer found, dissatisfaction, interruption or another cessation. It does not identify every no-referral search as a successful answer. [Fishkin, 2019, definition update].

The exact phrase zero-click visibility appears in decipher’s article by Ema Fulga. The current page shows **27 January 2026** and retains an earlier **26 September 2025** update block. That earlier displayed date is the earliest dated exact-phrase use we verified for this definition; it is not proof of coinage or an archived unchanged 2025 text. [Fulga, current page].

HubSpot’s AEO article also uses Zero-Click Visibility as a heading. On 30 October, its primary URL displayed **11 September and 26 October 2026** update dates in different responses. That conflict remains unresolved. These vendor uses establish terminology, not a common measurement standard or exposure value. [Clark, 2026].

## Define the missing click

“No click to our site” and “no click anywhere” are different outcomes. A person might visit a review platform, compare another vendor’s website, save a product description for later or return through a different route. A publisher’s analytics generally cannot observe all those actions.

Likewise, no recorded referral does not prove no visit occurred. Referrer handling, application transitions, consent and incomplete observation can prevent a visit from being attributed to the earlier answer. Use “unattributed” where that is the actual state of the evidence.

An archived answer that names a company establishes that the name appeared in the saved output. Without a linked behavioral record, it does not establish whether a human clicked or did not click afterward. Calling every such observation a zero-click event would overstate what was collected.

## Keep the reporting units apart

| Event | What would support it | What it leaves open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Brand named in an answer | Saved answer and explicit matching rule | Whether anyone viewed or acted on it |
| Source linked | Preserved citation destination | Whether the link was opened |
| Search impression | The platform’s stated impression definition | Complete attention or comprehension |
| Attributed website visit | A qualifying visit and attribution rule | The full earlier exposure history |
| Commercial outcome | A documented customer event | Whether this exposure caused it |

Google reports appearances in its AI Search features within overall Web performance data in Search Console. That is the operator’s reporting context; it is not a promise of a separate, complete person-level journey for each AI answer. [Google Search Central, measuring performance].

## What should change in a business report?

Show exposure and response in separate columns. A business can reasonably care about accurate representation before a visit, while still refusing to assign unobserved revenue to it. Negative, irrelevant or mistaken appearances also need to be distinguished from useful representation.

Avoid a universal conversion multiplier for no-click exposure. If a later survey asks how a customer first heard about a product, record the wording, timing and recall limits. If a comparison test estimates a commercial effect, report the design. A name in an answer remains a narrower observation until that additional evidence exists.

Rand Fishkin defines the historical event as “a search that results in zero website referrals”. That definition concerns observed referrals, leaving the reason for the search ending unresolved. [Fishkin, 13 August 2019, definition update after Methodology Notes; verified 30 October 2026].

You need referral observations to count clicks.

## What our own data shows

Source archive: [release 2026-09, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22907695](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22907695).

**Supports:** Study 2 found **5,477 named-without-own-domain-citation pairs among 42,792 eligible vendor-answer pairs: 12.8%, Wilson 95% interval 12.5% to 13.1%**. The [citation study](/research/studies/who-ai-engines-cite/) explains that denominator and exact matching rules.

This is a naming-without-own-citation result, **not a measured zero-click rate**. Another source could still be linked, and the archive contains no linked reader-click history. Our published method therefore keeps naming, own-domain citation and visitor behavior as separate concepts.

**Does not support:** Future rankings or a causal publishing effect.

**Suggests:** Follow-up within the stated setting.

# What is llms.txt, and what can it actually do?

**Google’s June 2026 guidance says llms.txt does not affect Search visibility or rankings; the proposal serves other possible uses (Google, 2026).**


Observed answers on stated dates, not a ranking.
Google’s **15 June 2026** documentation update says llms.txt files are not needed for Google Search and do not positively or negatively affect visibility or rankings. It also says maintaining them for other services is fine. That is narrower than saying that no software reads them. [Google Search Central, documentation updates](https://developers.google.com/search/updates).

The proposal itself has changed. Jeremy Howard’s current **v2**, modified **10 August 2026**, describes a concise Markdown guide that helps agents find information on a website. Read that revision before repeating instructions based on the initial proposal. The file is an emerging convention, not a rule that obliges every answer engine to read or obey it. [Howard, The /llms.txt file, v2](https://llmstxt.org/).

## Which kind of adoption can you verify?

Separate publication, retrieval, documented use and measured effect. A live file establishes that the publisher is serving it, whereas an HTTP request shows a requester asking for the file. A documented audit shows that a particular product checks it. None of those observations alone shows a resulting citation gain.

There is a concrete example of a reader: Chrome’s Lighthouse documentation describes its llms.txt audit. The audit flags a server error while retrieving the file; a missing file returning 404 is marked not applicable because the file is optional. This is evidence about that audit’s behaviour, not a Google Search ranking requirement. [Chrome for Developers, llms.txt audit, updated 5 May 2026](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/agentic-browsing/llms-txt).

The opened [FastHTML documentation file](https://www.fastht.ml/docs/llms.txt) is another inspectable publishing example. Its existence does not tell us which answer engines used it in a particular response. The proposal’s adoption examples should be read as named examples, rather than a census of all consumer behaviour.

## Choose a scope you can keep accurate

Under v2 a file can sit at the origin root or under a path. It covers URLs beneath that path, with a more specific applicable file taking precedence in the proposed convention. This makes a documentation section possible without requiring control over an entire shared hostname. [Howard, v2, proposal and format sections].

Decide what belongs in the guide before adding links. For a software documentation section, that may be the overview, terminology, supported versions and the pages people need to complete a task. For a research collection, prefer the methods, datasets, releases and correction policy that let a reader check the work, rather than an inventory whose only virtue is completeness. A short description of purpose can prevent the link list from becoming a second, less reliable sitemap.

Do not paste every page’s full text into the index because there is no immediate file-size error. The proposal’s intended reading path keeps the overview small and places detail behind links. A file that no one can review comfortably is also difficult to maintain responsibly.

## Write the smallest useful guide

The v2 format requires an H1 naming the site or project. It can then include a summary blockquote, explanatory text without intervening headings, and H2 sections containing linked file lists. An Optional section conventionally marks secondary material. The following is an **illustrative subset**, not a claim that the live Broadcastwell file consists only of these lines:

```markdown
# Broadcastwell research

> Dated evidence about software vendors named in AI answers.

The release identifier and capture date belong with each observation.

## Primary records

- [September Index](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22907695): Versioned data and method.
- [Research evidence standard](https://docs.broadcastwell.com/research/standard/): How claims are assessed.

## Optional

- [Absence Manual](https://docs.broadcastwell.com/): Longer explanations and references.
```

For a new file, prefer links whose labels say what a reader will find. Keep identity, scope and evidence limits visible. Do not use the file to insert instructions telling a third party to ignore its own safeguards, hide contrary evidence or favour your product irrespective of the question.

V2 also proposes clean Markdown versions of content pages and link relations identifying the alternate representation and the relevant guide. If you offer such links, verify that they resolve to the promised content. A renamed HTML response is not automatically a clean Markdown representation. [Howard, v2, proposal section].

## Inspect the file that is actually being served

Request the live URL and check its status, content type and text. A search engine’s cached extract can be older than the response a visitor receives. Compare the visible company description, dates and linked destinations with current public pages, then repair stale wording through the normal publishing process.

Our direct read of [docs.broadcastwell.com/llms.txt](https://docs.broadcastwell.com/llms.txt) on **30 October 2026** returned the current company description and dated terms. A search-cache version presented an older description. We therefore use the direct response as the worked publishing example. This is a content-consistency observation, not evidence that an AI answer consumed either version.

After a revision, read the file again from its public URL. Follow a sample of important links and any Markdown alternates you added. Check whether the file is still within the scope its path implies. If an item is a historical release, identify it as such rather than silently changing its label to “latest.”

## Keep discovery separate from permission

The proposal is intended to coexist with robots.txt, sitemaps and structured data. Those files do different jobs. A curated reading guide is not an access-control system, a complete crawl inventory or an authorization to reuse copyrighted material. Publishing a link cannot grant rights that the publisher does not hold. [Howard, v2, existing standards].

Keep private material out of every public representation. A file can reveal a link even if that link is absent from the human navigation. Check the full text, not merely the first screen. Where a document needs authentication, publishing an explanatory public page is a different choice from exposing the document itself.

## What would show that it helped?

Define the outcome before interpreting logs. A fetch of llms.txt, retrieval of a linked document, a source citation and a buyer visit are distinct events. A convincing effect claim would need a suitable comparison and a way to distinguish the file change from other changes to the site or engine. This guide supplies no such experiment.

For operational monitoring, report the observation you actually have: the requested path, period covered, stated requester identity and whether that identity was verified. Avoid saying that “AI reads our file” when the record only contains a matching user-agent string. The [crawler-log study](https://docs.broadcastwell.com/research/studies/ai-crawler-log/) explains that boundary.

Maintain llms.txt if it gives a useful, accurate route into your public material. Describe its intended use plainly. A current guide can be worthwhile without attaching an unsupported visibility promise to it.

Jeremy Howard describes the file as “A proposal to standardise”. That word matters: the proposal and an individual operator’s documented treatment of it remain separate sources of evidence. [Howard, The /llms.txt file, v2, opening description, modified 10 August 2026; verified 30 October 2026].

## What our own data shows

**Does not support:** We have no measurement on this point: whether serving our llms.txt changes citation or naming. Broadcastwell serves a public llms.txt file, which was opened directly for this guide. We have no measurement showing that the file increased our citations, naming rate or buyer visits. Presence and effect remain separate questions.

**Supports:** The initial crawler-log record covers selected public Index HTML routes. It is not a log of all requests to the documentation host or a proof of llms.txt consumption.

**Suggests:** Follow-up within the stated setting.

# How do you write a page an AI engine can quote?

**GEO’s best tested methods improved position-adjusted word-count visibility by 41%, not citation probability (Aggarwal et al., 2024, Table 1).**


Observed answers on stated dates, not a ranking.
**41%** is a result about a particular visibility metric in a particular experiment. It is not the probability that an AI engine will cite your next article. Aggarwal and colleagues report that the best tested methods improved position-adjusted word-count visibility by 41% and subjective impression by 28% against their benchmark baseline. The tested changes included statistics, quotations and source citations. [Aggarwal et al., 2024, Table 1 and §4](https://arxiv.org/html/2311.09735v3).

That is a useful reason to make evidence legible. It is not permission to attach an impressive number to a vague claim. The paper uses an experimental answer system and separately examines a deployed system; results depend on the metric, domain and method. Neither setting establishes a universal performance promise for a B2B product page published today.

The steps below are our editorial recommendations. They help a person check and quote a page. Their specific order, sentence length and layout have not been established as an optimal formula by that paper.

## Put the supported answer before the sales introduction

Begin with the question the page can actually answer. If the evidence only describes a captured sample, say so in the opening. A short result-first sentence gives readers something definite to assess; a broad claim about transforming an industry gives them much less.

For this section we use a quotable sentence of fewer than 30 words near the top. That is an editorial constraint, not a discovered engine threshold. Keep the source beside the sentence. If the source qualification will not fit, narrow the statement rather than removing the qualification.

Compare these fictional examples:

| Draft wording | What a reader needs |
|---|---|
| “Meridian Ledger is the market leader.” | A defined market, a dated measure and a primary basis for leadership. Without those, replace the claim. |
| “Meridian Ledger supports invoice export.” | A link to current product documentation, the export formats and any plan or configuration limits. |
| “Our test proves buyers prefer Meridian Ledger.” | Who the buyers were, how preference was measured, the comparison and the uncertainty. If the test measured mentions, say mentions. |

Meridian Ledger is an invented product. The examples show wording decisions; they report no product capabilities or observed experiment.

## Keep a number attached to what it measures

A useful statistical sentence names the outcome, population or archive, date, numerator and eligible base. Where observations are dependent, explain that dependence near the uncertainty estimate. A percentage alone is easy to quote and easy to misuse.

Do not turn a count of citations into a share of buyers. A linked URL, a publisher host, a vendor name and a vendor-answer pair are different units. Repeated appearances can matter, but a repeated-link count answers a different question from a distinct-host count. Choose the unit that matches the decision and label it consistently in the sentence, table and download.

If the primary source gives only a rounded percentage, do not invent an exact numerator by multiplying it by a sample size. Report what the paper actually supplies. If you recalculate a quantity from deposited data, show that it is your calculation and provide the inputs and formula.

The [quotable-number table](https://docs.broadcastwell.com/research/evidence/quotable-numbers/) illustrates this discipline. A limitation beside a result is part of the result a reader needs to carry forward.

## Make quotations recoverable

Name the speaker or author, identify the work and give the relevant page or section. Quote only the wording needed for the point. Ellipses should not hide a reversal, uncertainty or condition. A historical interview can explain how a practitioner thought; it cannot, by itself, prove how a current answer engine works.

An attributed quotation also needs an interpretable noun. “Visibility” may mean word-count share in an experimental answer, a captured mention rate, a search impression or a human visit. Preserve the source’s meaning before borrowing the term for a new context.

For numerical claims, link directly to the study, operator documentation or deposited data. A convenient summary can help a reader navigate, but the summary should not silently replace the original evidence. Where access is restricted, provide an authorized accessible original when one exists and keep the source identity intact.

## Write a section that survives being read alone

Use headings that state the reader’s question or the section’s plain claim. Define an abbreviation when its meaning matters. Give the object a clear name instead of repeatedly referring to “this,” especially when a table could be separated from the preceding paragraph.

Put a caption under a figure that explains the denominator, date and exclusions. A comparison should say whether the same questions, engines and configuration were used. If they differ, make those differences visible before discussing the resulting percentages.

This does not require repeating the whole method under every chart. It requires enough context that a chart does not become a different claim when shown in a slide. Provide the fuller method and data through stable links for anyone who needs to investigate.

## Expose the evidence in ordinary page text

Keep the main answer, table labels, source list and date visible without requiring a visitor to open an account. Use text navigation and descriptive links so that a reader can move from the assertion to its evidence. Check the page on a phone as well as a larger screen; a denominator hidden beyond an unmarked horizontal edge is easy to miss.

Use structured data to describe the visible content accurately. It cannot rescue a missing argument or supply a real-world result that the page does not establish. Google says the fundamentals of SEO remain relevant for its AI features and that no special additional optimization is necessary. That guidance concerns Google’s features, not every AI service. [Google Search Central, AI features and your website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features).

Before release, read the title, opening sentence and figure caption consecutively. Repair mismatched wording. Then follow the source links and check that each lands on the intended original.

## Date the evidence and define the next check

Show when the page was updated and when its sources were checked. A changed footer date is not evidence that a statistic was reverified. Maintain a correction note when a substantive result changes, retaining enough information for earlier readers to understand the difference.

Choose a next review based on what can change. A product capability may need checking after a release; a historical study’s published result is more stable, although a correction or a deposited calculation discrepancy can still matter. Do not let a current access date make an old observation sound newly measured.

Finally, keep the outcome claim modest. A well-supported page is easier for people to inspect and reuse. Whether a particular engine retrieves it, cites it or changes an answer remains an observation to measure later. Publishing the page does not complete that measurement.

Google Search Central states, “There are no additional technical requirements.” That sentence concerns eligibility for supporting links in Google AI features; it does not guarantee crawling, indexing or selection. [Google Search Central, AI features and your website, “Technical requirements for appearing in AI features”; verified 30 October 2026].

## What our own data shows

**Does not support:** We have no measurement on this point: the causal effect of this page format on citations or sales. Study 1 registers a descriptive test of observable signals on pages cited in the September Index. Its public plan distinguishes strong signals, weak signals, missing metadata and fetch failures. Those classes do not measure the causal benefit of rewriting a sentence.

**Supports:** We have no controlled measurement showing that this page format increases citations or sales. The released Index supplies dated naming and citation observations, which are a different outcome from an intervention effect.

**Suggests:** Follow-up within the stated setting.

# How do you write a page an AI engine can quote?

**Write a supported answer whose evidence, date and counted unit remain clear when the passage is read alone.**


Observed answers on stated dates, not a ranking.
Aggarwal and colleagues tested statistics, quotations and source citations in an experimental answer system using position-adjusted word-count visibility and subjective impressions. Those measures are not the probability that an AI engine will cite a newly published B2B page. [Aggarwal et al., 2024, Table 1 and §4](https://arxiv.org/html/2311.09735v3).

The paper’s main result and five-seed appendix do not report the same estimates. We treat that headline as fragile rather than adopting it as a publishing effect. The paper also examines a deployed system, where results vary by method. Neither setting establishes a universal performance promise for a B2B page.

The steps below are our editorial recommendations. They help a person check and quote a page. Their specific order, sentence length and layout have not been established as an optimal formula by that paper.

## Put the supported answer before the sales introduction

Begin with the question the page can actually answer. If the evidence only describes a captured sample, say so in the opening. A short result-first sentence gives readers something definite to assess; a broad claim about transforming an industry gives them much less.

For this section we use a quotable sentence of fewer than 30 words near the top. That is an editorial constraint, not a discovered engine threshold. Keep the source beside the sentence. If the source qualification will not fit, narrow the statement rather than removing the qualification.

Compare these fictional examples:

| Draft wording | What a reader needs |
|---|---|
| “Meridian Ledger is the market leader.” | A defined market, a dated measure and a primary basis for leadership. Without those, replace the claim. |
| “Meridian Ledger supports invoice export.” | A link to current product documentation, the export formats and any plan or configuration limits. |
| “Our test proves buyers prefer Meridian Ledger.” | Who the buyers were, how preference was measured, the comparison and the uncertainty. If the test measured mentions, say mentions. |

Meridian Ledger is an invented product. The examples show wording decisions; they report no product capabilities or observed experiment.

## Keep a number attached to what it measures

A useful statistical sentence names the outcome, population or archive, date, numerator and eligible base. Where observations are dependent, explain that dependence near the uncertainty estimate. A percentage alone is easy to quote and easy to misuse.

Do not turn a count of citations into a share of buyers. A linked URL, a publisher host, a vendor name and a vendor-answer pair are different units. Repeated appearances can matter, but a repeated-link count answers a different question from a distinct-host count. Choose the unit that matches the decision and label it consistently in the sentence, table and download.

If the primary source gives only a rounded percentage, do not invent an exact numerator by multiplying it by a sample size. Report what the paper actually supplies. If you recalculate a quantity from deposited data, show that it is your calculation and provide the inputs and formula.

The [quotable-number table](https://docs.broadcastwell.com/research/evidence/quotable-numbers/) illustrates this discipline. A limitation beside a result is part of the result a reader needs to carry forward.

## Make quotations recoverable

Name the speaker or author, identify the work and give the relevant page or section. Quote only the wording needed for the point. Ellipses should not hide a reversal, uncertainty or condition. A historical interview can explain how a practitioner thought; it cannot, by itself, prove how a current answer engine works.

An attributed quotation also needs an interpretable noun. “Visibility” may mean word-count share in an experimental answer, a captured mention rate, a search impression or a human visit. Preserve the source’s meaning before borrowing the term for a new context.

For numerical claims, link directly to the study, operator documentation or deposited data. A convenient summary can help a reader navigate, but the summary should not silently replace the original evidence. Where access is restricted, provide an authorized accessible original when one exists and keep the source identity intact.

## Write a section that survives being read alone

Use headings that state the reader’s question or the section’s plain claim. Define an abbreviation when its meaning matters. Give the object a clear name instead of repeatedly referring to “this,” especially when a table could be separated from the preceding paragraph.

Put a caption under a figure that explains the denominator, date and exclusions. A comparison should say whether the same questions, engines and configuration were used. If they differ, make those differences visible before discussing the resulting percentages.

This does not require repeating the whole method under every chart. It requires enough context that a chart does not become a different claim when shown in a slide. Provide the fuller method and data through stable links for anyone who needs to investigate.

## Expose the evidence in ordinary page text

Keep the main answer, table labels, source list and date visible without requiring a visitor to open an account. Use text navigation and descriptive links so that a reader can move from the assertion to its evidence. Check the page on a phone as well as a larger screen; a denominator hidden beyond an unmarked horizontal edge is easy to miss.

Use structured data to describe the visible content accurately. It cannot rescue a missing argument or supply a real-world result that the page does not establish. Google says the fundamentals of SEO remain relevant for its AI features and that no special additional optimization is necessary. That guidance concerns Google’s features, not every AI service. [Google Search Central, AI features and your website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features).

Before release, read the title, opening sentence and figure caption consecutively. Repair mismatched wording. Then follow the source links and check that each lands on the intended original.

## Date the evidence and define the next check

Show when the page was updated and when its sources were checked. A changed footer date is not evidence that a statistic was reverified. Maintain a correction note when a substantive result changes, retaining enough information for earlier readers to understand the difference.

Choose a next review based on what can change. A product capability may need checking after a release; a historical study’s published result is more stable, although a correction or a deposited calculation discrepancy can still matter. Do not let a current access date make an old observation sound newly measured.

Finally, keep the outcome claim modest. A well-supported page is easier for people to inspect and reuse. Whether a particular engine retrieves it, cites it or changes an answer remains an observation to measure later. Publishing the page does not complete that measurement.

Google Search Central states, “There are no additional technical requirements.” That sentence concerns eligibility for supporting links in Google AI features; it does not guarantee crawling, indexing or selection. [Google Search Central, AI features and your website, “Technical requirements for appearing in AI features”; verified 30 October 2026].

## What our own data shows

**Does not support:** We have no measurement on this point: the causal effect of this page format on citations or sales. Study 1 registers a descriptive test of observable signals on pages cited in the September Index. Its public plan distinguishes strong signals, weak signals, missing metadata and fetch failures. Those classes do not measure the causal benefit of rewriting a sentence.

**Supports:** We have no controlled measurement showing that this page format increases citations or sales. The released Index supplies dated naming and citation observations, which are a different outcome from an intervention effect.

A worked example from our [published citation study](/research/studies/who-ai-engines-cite/) is: 39 of 2,095 eligible target answers captured on 22 and 23 September 2026 had empty supplied citation lists, 1.9%, with a descriptive 95% Wilson interval of 1.4% to 2.5%. The [answer-base table](/research/data/answer-citation-bases.csv) makes the unit and denominator recoverable. This sentence illustrates how to report our own count; it does not show that this writing format earns a citation, or that those answers used no underlying sources.

# How can research become discoverable in Scholar and Dataset Search?

**Rovira’s two-term Google Scholar correlations were 0.721 unrestricted and 0.994 title-restricted; they do not establish an inclusion tactic (2019, Table 2).**


Observed answers on stated dates, not a ranking.
**0.721 and 0.994** are the correlations Rovira and colleagues report for their two-term Google Scholar searches under unrestricted and title-restricted conditions. They compare search order with aggregated citation-based ranks in that historical design. They do not estimate the benefit of adding a keyword to your paper’s title, and they are not acceptance probabilities. [Rovira et al., 2019, Table 2, reprint PDF p. 56].

The practical task is more basic: make the work identifiable, accessible and accurately described for the discovery system concerned. Google Scholar’s scholarly-document guidelines and Google Dataset Search’s dataset metadata address different objects. A research report can accompany a dataset without becoming the dataset itself.

## Decide what each landing page represents

Use a report page for an argument with methods, findings, limitations and references. Use a dataset page for a defined collection of observations or records, with its variables, creator, version, license and downloadable distributions. Connect them through explicit links rather than describing either as everything at once.

A product brochure with citations is not automatically a scholarly paper. A PDF extension alone does not establish scholarly content. Google Scholar’s inclusion guidelines describe the content and technical conditions its indexing system expects. Read those before promising a marketing team that a deposit will appear there. [Google Scholar, Inclusion guidelines for webmasters].

A dataset likewise needs an actual collection that another reader can understand and obtain under its stated conditions. An attractive chart with no recoverable observations is not equivalent to an accessible dataset release.

## Prepare the report for a reader and a parser

Put the paper’s title prominently on its first page, with authors beneath it and a recognizable references section later. Provide selectable text rather than an image-only scan. Keep the abstract and full-text link visible on a stable article page. These are practical checks drawn from Scholar’s content and indexing guidance, not a guarantee of admission.

Use consistent bibliographic metadata across the landing page, PDF and repository deposit. A title that differs substantially between those surfaces makes the identity harder to check. Author order and publication date should describe the same work rather than a mixture of an old manuscript and a later dataset.

Review the exported PDF itself. Copy a passage to check that the text is recoverable, inspect tables for cut-off labels and follow its references. A browser preview that looks polished can still conceal a poor text layer. Keep the source inspectable.

## Give crawlers a simple route to the work

Scholar’s guidance emphasizes ordinary HTML links and a browse interface. A small publication list can link directly to each report and its full text. Do not require a form submission or account just to discover the abstract and title. A search box by itself is not a reliable substitute for a crawlable publication list. [Google Scholar, crawl guidelines].

Check that the article page and PDF respond consistently. If a work moves, provide an appropriate redirect to its new location rather than sending every old article link to a generic homepage. Preserve a useful abstract or explanation for someone arriving from an old citation.

Look for accidental robots restrictions and server errors, while retaining appropriate access controls for private material. Publication for indexing should be deliberate. Do not remove authentication from a private dataset simply to make a discovery check pass.

## Describe the data with Dataset metadata

Google’s Dataset guide explains how supporting information such as a name, description, creator and distribution format can help Dataset Search find a collection. It also describes identifiers, licenses, related works and download metadata. Encode facts that agree with the visible page. [Google Search Central, Dataset structured data].

| Metadata question | A useful answer |
|---|---|
| What is this collection? | A specific name and description of the measured unit and scope. |
| Which version is being described? | A stable version identifier, including a DOI where assigned. |
| Who created and publishes it? | The actual creators and publisher, consistently identified. |
| What can a reader download? | A distribution link with the real format and accessible destination. |
| What reuse is allowed? | The applicable license and any material restrictions. |
| Which report explains the work? | A related scholarly work, distinct from the dataset’s own citation identity. |

The guide specifically recommends using identifier for relevant DOIs. Do not place the dataset’s own citation solely in a property intended for a related article. A correct identifier helps locate the object; it does not endorse the data or their interpretation.

## Keep the deposited object and its versions distinct

A repository record provides a durable place to identify files and their authorship. Before release, check that the advertised CSVs are attached, their headers match the variable description and the license covers what you are distributing. Do not upload restricted third-party books merely because the analysis discusses them.

When a record distinguishes a version DOI from a concept or record-family DOI, use the version DOI for the exact inputs behind a numerical result. The family identifier can guide readers toward later versions. Label the two clearly rather than letting a citation silently change its underlying files.

For Broadcastwell’s worked example, the [September Index version](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22907695) contains the release and archived answers used by the research pages. The [August version](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22721962) identifies a different release and configuration. Their DOI identities do not make them interchangeable experimental conditions.

## Keep academic-search ranking separate from inclusion

Rovira’s comparison is about ordering in academic search systems, not ordinary web rankings or inclusion in Dataset Search. Its stronger title-restricted association does not mean repeating a title keyword generates citations. The query restriction changes which results are being compared. [Rovira et al., 2019, methods and Table 2].

There is also a deposited calculation discrepancy in the one-term title-restricted workbook. Our [source review](https://docs.broadcastwell.com/research/sources/rovira-2019/) explains that discrepancy and links the reanalysis. It does not change the two-term figures quoted above, but it reinforces why a neat headline should not replace a check of the actual calculation.

Use a precise title because it describes the work accurately. Do not add irrelevant phrases, inflate the claimed outcome or confuse a topic with an experimentally supported finding in order to chase a presumed discovery advantage.

## Verify inclusion separately from submission

After publishing, test the public URLs and metadata. Then search for the exact title in Scholar and the appropriate dataset identity in Dataset Search. Record the date, query and matching result. A general Google result for the landing page is not proof of Scholar or Dataset Search inclusion.

An absent result on a single check means inclusion was not observed in that search at that time. It does not prove a permanent rejection or diagnose the cause. Recheck the relevant guidelines and technical access, preserve the observation and allow for processing rather than repeatedly changing the title without evidence.

Report the states separately: deposited, publicly accessible, metadata validated, found in the relevant discovery service and cited by another work. Each requires its own evidence. That separation leaves the research record useful even while indexing remains unconfirmed.

Google Scholar says, “Each paper must have its own unique URL”. That requirement concerns the discoverable paper itself; it does not turn a catalogue entry or a dataset description into a scholarly article. [Google Scholar, Inclusion guidelines, “Preparing article URLs”; verified 30 October 2026].

## What our own data shows

**Does not support:** We have no measurement on this point: whether this new research section has gained inclusion because of the proposed publishing changes. Our source review reproduces the historical academic-search calculation from the authors’ deposited workbooks, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.3381151. That reanalysis is distinct from measuring whether our own research appears in Google Scholar or Dataset Search.

**Supports:** We have no verified inclusion result for this new research section in either discovery service at the time of writing. Existing Zenodo DOI records establish deposited identities and files, not a visibility gain from those deposits.

**Suggests:** Follow-up within the stated setting.

# Which site-structure basics still matter?

**A page that says “not found” while returning HTTP 200 can be treated as a soft 404 (Google Crawling Infrastructure, 2026).**


Observed answers on stated dates, not a ranking.
A **200 response is not proof of a useful page or indexing**. Google’s current status-code documentation explains that content suggesting an error or empty page can be classified as a soft 404 even when the server returns success. A visible apology alone does not make a missing-page response technically correct. [Google Crawling Infrastructure, HTTP status codes](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/troubleshooting/http-status-codes).

Site structure gives a reader stable destinations and an intelligible route among them. It also gives crawlers addresses they can request. The checks below are practical ways to preserve those properties. They do not establish that a particular URL pattern causes a higher AI citation rate.

## Give each substantive page a preferred address

Decide which URL represents the page and use it consistently in internal links, the sitemap and relevant metadata. Keep tracking parameters out of the address you present as the permanent reference when those parameters do not change the content. A citation should continue to identify the same page after a campaign ends.

Google’s current canonical guidance distinguishes redirects, canonical annotations and sitemap signals. These communicate a preference while Google still makes its own selection. Do not promise that a tag forces a particular outcome. [Google Search Central, canonical URL guidance].

“One page, one preferred URL” is a useful publishing rule, rather than a claim that all alternate representations are forbidden. Language versions, downloads and genuine product variants can require distinct addresses. Explain the relationship instead of redirecting every alternative to an unrelated homepage.

The 2010 guide already advised concentrating on one URL when the same content was accessible through multiple addresses. Its historical recommendation belongs beside current canonical guidance, not in place of it. [Google, 2010, PDF p. 9].

## Make the address recognizable when copied

Use a readable path that describes the page’s subject. Avoid meaningless identifiers where a useful descriptive slug is practical, and avoid placing essential identity only in a long query string. A reader who receives a shortened display of a URL should still have a reasonable clue about its destination.

Google’s current URL guide recommends hyphens to separate words and explains that case differences can identify different URLs. It also recommends reducing unnecessary parameters and avoiding fragment-driven content changes. These are specific crawlability and clarity points; they do not establish a maximum SEO-friendly title length. [URL structure best practices].

Test the actual address in the places people use it: a document reference, a phone message and a search-result preview. “Truncation-safe” here means our editorial preference for recognizable, stable paths, not an operator-defined metric or a promise that every interface will show the same number of characters.

## Use breadcrumbs that match the page’s place

Show the route from a broader topic to the current page when that route helps the visitor. For this research section, a source review belongs under the research and sources context, while a study has its own study identity. Avoid breadcrumbs that point to unrelated product categories simply to insert desired words.

The 2010 guide describes breadcrumbs as a way to navigate back toward a more general section. Google’s current structured-data guide separately describes BreadcrumbList for a page’s navigational context. Keep the visible links and encoded representation consistent. [Google, 2010, PDF p. 10; Google Search Central, Breadcrumb structured data].

Follow the links after publication. A syntactically valid breadcrumb with a missing parent destination still disappoints a reader. An accurate navigational trail is useful even when no special search display appears.

## Return a real error for a missing page

A missing page should have an appropriate not-found response and a helpful explanation. Offer useful navigation without pretending that the requested content exists. A redirect is appropriate when there is a genuine replacement, rather than as a way to send every obsolete URL to the homepage.

Google distinguishes not-found responses from server failures and rate-limit signals. Its documentation says success responses can be considered for processing, while indexing remains unguaranteed. Use the status that describes the actual condition instead of choosing one solely because a dashboard shows fewer errors. [Google Crawling Infrastructure, HTTP status codes].

For a practical check, request a known page, an intentionally nonexistent path and any moved page. Inspect both the response code and the visible content. A custom error design can be pleasant to use while still returning the correct status.

## Make links work as links

Google’s link guide says crawlable anchors generally need an HTML a element with an href. A script event on a styled span is a different object. Where interactive navigation is needed, preserve a sensible ordinary link destination as well. [Google Search Central, Link best practices].

Check important routes without depending on a search form or a hidden menu. A visitor should be able to move from the section hub to an individual page and then to its evidence. Give the site a clear hierarchy.

The historical guide’s recommendation for mostly text navigation remains a useful principle, even though its examples name older technologies. Read it as a reason to provide usable links, then verify behaviour in the current site. [Google, 2010, PDF p. 12].

## Write anchors that identify the destination

Prefer a phrase such as “September citation-class table” when that is what the link opens. A page filled with repeated “click here” labels makes it difficult to understand destinations out of context. Google’s current guide recommends descriptive, reasonably concise anchor text relevant to both pages. [Link best practices, anchor text].

Do not fill every anchor with a long string of targeted terms. A useful link label sets an expectation for a human reader. The sentence around it can supply additional context when the destination is a dataset, historical source or download rather than another article.

For images used as links, provide text that explains the destination through the appropriate accessible representation. A decorative graphic should not become the only intelligible way to navigate to a substantive page.

## Check the whole route after an edit

| Check | What success establishes | What it does not establish |
|---|---|---|
| Preferred URL and response | The intended public page can be reached | Search indexing or canonical selection by an engine. |
| Canonical annotation | The page communicates its preferred identity | A binding instruction to every search system. |
| Breadcrumb and topic links | Readers can move through the published hierarchy | A quantified ranking advantage from that hierarchy. |
| Missing-path response | Absent content is represented honestly | A cure for unrelated discovery or quality problems. |
| Descriptive anchors | A reader can anticipate linked material | That the destination’s claim is factually correct. |

Run these checks on the deployed pages after a navigation change, as well as on a local preview. A broken link can survive a successful build. Keep any observed indexing state separate from these technical and editorial checks.

Google’s link guidance says, “Good anchor text is descriptive, reasonably concise”. The surrounding explanation also asks that the wording fit both the current page and the linked destination. [Google Search Central, Link best practices, “Write good anchor text”; verified 30 October 2026].

## What our own data shows

**Does not support:** We have no measurement on this point: the causal citation effect of these site-structure changes. The Index’s archived answers can identify which URLs were visibly cited on stated dates. They do not expose every retrieval step or establish that a breadcrumb, slug or response code caused selection.

**Supports:** No causal effect was measured. Their immediate purpose is to keep public pages reachable, understandable and accurately identified.

**Suggests:** Follow-up within the stated setting.

# Which structured data belongs on a B2B software site?

**Google stopped showing FAQ rich results from 7 May 2026; FAQPage remains a Schema.org type (Google, 2026; Schema.org, 2026).**


Observed answers on stated dates, not a ranking.
Google gives **7 May 2026** for the end of FAQ rich-result display; its later documentation update explains why the former FAQ feature page was removed. A Schema.org type can remain meaningful even after a search feature stops using it in that way. [Google Search Central, May 8 and June 15 changelog entries](https://developers.google.com/search/updates); [Schema.org, FAQPage](https://schema.org/FAQPage).

For a B2B software site, start with what the page actually describes. An organization, a software application, a product offer, a dataset and a navigation trail are different things. Marking all of them on every page makes the representation less useful. Choose the type and properties that match the visible material, then check the requirements of the service you hope will consume them.

## Match the entity before choosing properties

| Visible subject | Appropriate starting point | What to establish first |
|---|---|---|
| The company itself | Organization | Consistent name, official site and an identity that the page supports. |
| A particular software application | SoftwareApplication, or an appropriate subtype | The application’s own name and factual capabilities; distinguish the app from its publisher. |
| A product or commercial offer | Product and, where appropriate, Offer | What is actually offered, the current terms and whether the chosen Google feature supports that content. |
| A page of published questions and answers | FAQPage | The questions and answers are really on the page; do not promise a retired Google rich result. |
| A published research dataset | Dataset, with DataDownload for its files | Name, description, creator, identifier, license, access and distribution details. |
| The route through a site | BreadcrumbList | A real, ordered navigation trail with resolvable destinations. |

The table is a planning aid. That vocabulary does not confer Google eligibility. The broad Schema.org vocabulary and Google’s supported feature requirements are separate references.

## Give the organization a stable identity

Google’s Organization documentation explains that organization markup can help it understand administrative details and distinguish similarly named entities. Use an official name and website that agree with the company’s visible facts. A stable identifier can connect references to the same organization across pages. [Google Search Central, Organization structured data].

Avoid making a department, a product and the legal company share a name merely for convenience. Describe their actual relationship. Link to a profile as an identity reference only when it identifies the same entity. A page that mentions the company is not automatically an equivalent identity page.

Do not add an award, partner status, address or service area because another site with a similar name has one. Evidence still comes before markup. If a fact cannot be supported in ordinary prose, encoding it out of sight does not make it safer to assert.

## Separate an application from a price claim

SoftwareApplication describes software. Google’s current software-app rich-result requirements include a name, an offer price and a rating or review, with further rules for those properties. An application description that is valid in the vocabulary may therefore remain ineligible for that specific search appearance. [Google Search Central, Software app structured data, required properties].

Do not invent a zero price for a product that requires a commercial agreement. Likewise, do not make up a star rating to satisfy a required field. If the real offer lacks the data needed for a feature, leave the feature unclaimed. The application can still have an accurate page.

When prices or plans change, review both the visible page and the embedded data. An old number can survive in a template after the public table has changed. Inspect the rendered page rather than assuming that a successful content edit updated every representation.

## Describe a dataset so a reader can obtain it

A dataset landing page should identify the collection before it lists files. State what the rows represent, who created the data, which version is being described and what license permits reuse. Link the actual download separately from the explanation of the method. Google’s Dataset guide recommends identifiers such as DOIs and describes distribution metadata. [Google Search Central, Dataset structured data].

Here is an invented illustration of a small research release. This example reports no measurement:

```json
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Dataset",
  "name": "Example invoice-format observations",
  "description": "Illustrative metadata only; not an actual dataset.",
  "creator": {"@type": "Organization", "name": "Example Research"},
```

Executive decision

Fictional buyer: a small laboratory evaluating formulation-record software. The strongest supported issue is a contradiction between the exercise integration draft and its product sheet. Prepare a bounded clarification of connector type and edition requirements. No observation establishes that this wording caused an absence, that any real engine would respond differently, or that a sale was lost.

Priority order: DEMO-WO-01 fixes the direct integration contradiction; DEMO-WO-02 adds missing prerequisites; DEMO-WO-03 prepares a source-name correction for later authorized review. Implementation and any live review session are separate unless expressly included in the actual engagement. No purchase is justified by these fictional measurements.

Actual fixture coverage

Six authored observation slots; three completed; one failed; one untested; one uncertain. Of the completed records, one has a reviewed present mention, one a reviewed absent mention and one awaits classification. The reviewed mention denominator is two. This small synthetic set has no population, independent-buyer or real performance interpretation.

All records use engine fictional-test-surface, interface local-fixture, provider null, method synthetic-example-v1. Locale context: en-US fictional exercise; times are fixture metadata on September 24, 2026. No provider calls ran. The question IDs and receipt IDs are preserved in the exact JSON appendix. This six-slot teaching fixture does not replace any contracted Audit measurement allowance.

What the evidence supports

Finding F-01: DEMO-RECEIPT-001 names Northstar Lab and describes connector-based export. That is a present mention, not a recommendation. Separately DEMO-PAGE-01 says native on every plan, while DEMO-FACT-01/02 state third-party connector, Team edition and separate account. This independent conflict supports reviewing the draft wording; it does not establish a ranking cause.

Finding F-02: DEMO-RECEIPT-002 omits the current and former fictional names in a completed reviewed answer about migration. No cause is known. DEMO-PAGE-02 separately omits edition/account prerequisites supplied by DEMO-FACT-02. Missing page detail is distinguished from a false statement.

Finding F-03: DEMO-PAGE-03 uses the former name as current, while DEMO-FACT-03 distinguishes them. A correction draft is supported. No request was sent and no listing changed. Historical records retain their original names.

Three implementation-ready proposals

DEMO-WO-01 , Clarify third-party integration scope (P1)

Direct contradiction could misstate compatibility and edition fit.

Affected fixture URL: https://example.com/demo/integrations/atlas. Evidence: DEMO-PAGE-01, DEMO-FACT-01, DEMO-FACT-02.

Proposed change: Replace the unsupported draft with: “Export to Atlas Analytics through the third-party BridgeKit connector. Requires Northstar Lab Team edition and a separately configured BridgeKit account. Confirm the documented prerequisites before setup.” Link the approved exercise product sheet; do not state a price or activation time.

Scope: One integration paragraph and its duplicated on-page summary; no connector implementation or new page allowance.

Dependencies: Current approved product fact version; Authorized page owner and scoped allowance; Existing release path and preview.

Recommended role: Product content editor; technical/product reviewer. Real owner, approver and due date remain unassigned.

Acceptance:

  • Native and every-plan claims removed from the scoped paragraph and its duplicated summary.
  • Connector type, Team edition and separate account prerequisite visible together.
  • Source version DEMO-DOC-01 is linked in the implementation record; fictional product reviewer role checks every factual clause.
  • Keyboard-accessible source link; no overflow at 360, 768 and 1440 pixels.
  • Fictional status remains in the page preview and export.

Recheck: After actual publication evidence, product approval and a separately authorized matching question/method recheck.

Rollback: Restore only the changed paragraph from the owner-recorded previous page revision. Preserve legitimate unrelated changes.

DEMO-WO-02 , State edition and account prerequisites (P2)

Missing prerequisites can leave an evaluator unable to assess edition fit; no contradictory price is established.

Affected fixture URL: https://example.com/demo/editions. Evidence: DEMO-PAGE-02, DEMO-FACT-02.

Proposed change: Add below the BridgeKit export description: “Available for Northstar Lab Team edition in this fictional catalogue. A separately configured BridgeKit account is required. Price and setup timing are not specified in this exercise; confirm current terms before deciding.” Preserve all existing price and contract fields.

Scope: One explanatory block; no price, contract, credit, guarantee or purchased allowance change.

Dependencies: DEMO-FACT-02; Unchanged current commercial record; Page owner review.

Recommended role: Product content editor; commercial reviewer. Real owner, approver and due date remain unassigned.

Acceptance:

  • Edition and account dependency are stated beside export wording.
  • No added numeric price, discount, guarantee or timing promise.
  • Unknown price and timing remain unknown; commercial reviewer approval required before real adaptation.
  • Existing commercial fields preserved in diff; source and synthetic labels retained.

Recheck: Only after the edition block is publicly accessible and relevant comparable scope is approved.

Rollback: Revert the bounded explanatory block using the recorded prior page revision.

DEMO-WO-03 , Prepare a current-name correction (P3)

Independent listing name conflict is supported, but a third-party change depends on its owner.

# The three measured rates

These definitions describe the Category Audit's three reported measures. Named and cited as a source use the valid captured answers. Share of voice uses the brand mentions recorded in those answers. Each has its own count and denominator. We never add or weight the measures into a composite score.

## Named

An answer counts once when it names the company. The denominator is the valid answer base for the total, engine or question group being reported. A full Category Audit schedules 150 observations: ten questions on ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode, with three runs of each question. Failed or empty observations are excluded from the answer base and reported separately.

## Cited as a source

An answer counts once when at least one listed source is on the company's own website domain or a confirmed alias, including its subdomains. It uses the same valid answer base as named. The cited source list is the evidence; we do not infer a citation from an uncited mention in the answer text.

## Share of voice

The numerator is the answers naming the company. The denominator is the mentions of the company and the recorded rivals across the same valid answers, with each brand counted once per answer. This covers the brands recorded for the order, not every brand in the market. It is a share of brand mentions, not a percentage of answers.

## Record accuracy, when classified

The report identifies which company or recorded rival each classified statement describes, and counts statements classed correct, wrong or stale against the dated public evidence. An unverified or unclassified statement is not automatically wrong. A classification remains provisional until its team review is recorded. When no classification exists, the report does not imply a zero error count.

## Attribute profile, when classified

Recorded descriptions of the company and its rivals carry the number of supporting answers and a receipt. Unreviewed rows are labelled: “From the captured answers; provisional until reviewed.” The profile does not imply that every rival or every possible attribute was assessed.

## Scope and related rules

These descriptive measures are separate from the Fix Sprint payment tests in the [current terms](https://broadcastwell.com/terms). Those tests use named answers, cited as a source and record accuracy; share of voice is not a payment test. The wider 35 question program method and historical measurements retain their own scope.

The [Kalvenor findings sample](https://app.broadcastwell.com/sample/findings) uses fictional **SAMPLE DATA** to show the reporting format. Its figures do not describe a real customer or a future result.

The separate [bot access resource](bot-access.md) explains the limits of server requests and HTML checks. These rates measure captured answers; they do not establish why a source was chosen or what a buyer did next.

[Every figure comes from the published method, v1.1.](https://broadcastwell.com/methodology)

# Why does ChatGPT not mention us?

Usually because the sources the engine reads in your category name someone else. The engine is not weighing your product against theirs. It is assembling an answer out of pages it can reach and treats as reliable, and if those pages name three vendors and you are not one of them, you are not in the answer. The same holds for Claude, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode, which most buyers call Gemini.

Four causes account for almost every case we measure. They are not mutually exclusive, and the fix for one does nothing for the others.

## 1. The sources the engines read in your category do not name you

When an engine answers a buyer question, it leans on a small and surprisingly stable set of pages: comparison articles, category roundups, review sites, a handful of publications. Those pages are where the vendor names come from. If the three or four sources an engine reads for your category list your competitors and not you, the engine has nothing to name you with.

What changes it: being named on those specific sources. Not on every surface a company could be mentioned, but on the ones the engines are actually reading in your category, which is a measurement question before it is a placement question.

## 2. Your entity facts are thin or inconsistent across the web

An engine has to be confident it knows who you are before it will put you in front of a buyer. When your own site, your directory listings and your social profiles disagree about what you do, who you serve or even what you are called, that confidence is low, and a low-confidence vendor is left out of a short answer.

What changes it: one consistent account of the company across everything you own, with ordinary structured data of the kind the engines already read. Nothing AI-specific is required for this.

## 3. The engines cannot reach your site at all

Hosting rules, security settings and bot filters block AI crawlers silently. The site is up, visitors can read it, analytics look healthy, and most visibility tools will report nothing wrong, because they are not the crawler being blocked. This is the cheapest cause to rule out and the one most often missed.

What changes it: a pass or fail check of crawler access, then a change to the hosting or security rule that is refusing the request.

## 4. You are present on how-to questions and absent on shortlist questions

Not every question is the same question. A buyer asking how to solve a problem gets a different answer from a buyer asking who to buy from. Being cited on the first kind and absent from the second is the most common shape we find, and it is why a company can watch its mentions rise and see nothing change in its pipeline.

What changes it: knowing which questions you lose, by type, rather than a single visibility number that averages the two together.

## How to find out which one applies to you

The four causes look identical from the outside. The only way to tell them apart is to put the same buyer questions to every engine, more than once, and record what comes back: who is named instead of you, how often, and which pages the engines read to name them. That is what the [$490 Category Audit](https://broadcastwell.com/pricing) does, on one category and ten buyer questions across five engines with three measured runs each, and it checks crawler access first.

## What nobody can promise you

No one can guarantee that an engine will name you, or place you first, or send you a given number of leads. Any supplier who offers that is selling something they cannot deliver. What can be done is honest and narrow: measure where you stand on a fixed question set, name the specific sources and pages responsible, change them, and measure the same set again.

# Why does ChatGPT not mention us?

Start with the dated answer and its context to investigate an omission. Our records retain named products and explicit source links; they do not expose every source an engine considered or establish why it omitted a company. The September Index keeps ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode separate, so an observation from one surface should not stand in for them all.

The four checks below organize possible explanations. Our answer records do not establish how common each explanation is or whether a particular change will affect the next answer. More than one check may be relevant to the same page.

## 1. Check the visible sources for your company name

Open the sources explicitly cited in the retained answer, whether they are comparison articles, category roundups, review sites or other publications. Check whether they name the intended company and support the statements at issue. The visible list does not reveal every source considered, and a missing name on those pages does not explain the omission by itself.

We can check a specific inaccurate or incomplete public statement and the evidence needed to correct it. A later naming or citation result needs its own dated observation; a source change alone does not establish that result.

## 2. Compare your public company facts

Compare the company and product names, category and official website across the public records concerned. Conflicting statements can be documented and checked against dated evidence. An omitted name does not reveal an engine’s internal confidence or prove that identity confusion caused the omission.

We can correct supported company facts on pages we control, following the relevant provider’s documented requirements. Keep the source and date with each correction. We have no measured confidence increase or assured naming result from making those statements consistent.

## 3. Check access for the relevant page and requester

A failed request and a page opening in a human browser are different observations. Check the intended URL, the requesting service’s documented identity, the response and any applicable access rule. A user-agent label alone does not authenticate the service. Our answer records do not establish how often access failures cause omissions or how often other tools miss them.

We can check the response to a specific verified request against the intended access policy. Where that evidence supports an authorized rule change, read the result back and report access separately from later naming or citation outcomes.

## 4. Compare the question types in your retained answers

Count naming and citation under the stated rule for each retained question. An explanatory question and a supplier-shortlist question can return different products and sources. Compare their actual answers before describing that pattern. Those records do not establish what happened to a buyer’s pipeline or sales.

We can check which questions produced answers naming or omitting your company, with the engine, valid answer base and collection date recorded.

## How to record what you find

Start with fixed buyer questions and repeated, dated answers, retaining the named vendors and explicit source links. Those records describe the outputs to inspect. Access checks and source-fact checks need their own evidence; repeated answers alone do not identify a cause. That is what the [Absence Index](https://index.broadcastwell.com/) records for its 14 categories, and what the [Fix Sprint](https://broadcastwell.com/answer-repair) ($3,900) measures in its first phase for your own category: ten buyer questions across five engines with three measured runs each, with crawler access checked first.

## What our observations cannot promise

Our dated observations do not promise future naming, first placement or leads. We can define a question set, retain answers and visible sources, and identify supported page corrections. A later matched observation can describe a difference; it does not, by itself, prove that the correction caused it. Assess any separate commercial promise against its written terms and evidence.
